slides.title: Three pillars
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.picture: Three columns rise one at a time and a roof rests on them.

new_texts: A game rests on the player's role, communication and appeal.
What the player does and why; the player, not the game, drives it forward.
Player: the player has a role and a purpose, and drives the game. Without that they just complete tasks.
all_texts: A game rests on the player's role, communication and appeal.
What the player does and why; the player, not the game, drives it forward.
Player: the player has a role and a purpose, and drives the game. Without that they just complete tasks.

new_texts: Communication: without it the player does not know the goal or how to reach it, and feels powerless.
all_texts: A game rests on the player's role, communication and appeal.
What the player does and why; the player, not the game, drives it forward.
Communication: without it the player does not know the goal or how to reach it, and feels powerless.

new_texts: Appeal: the pull to keep playing. It is the hardest to guarantee, and the most important.
all_texts: A game rests on the player's role, communication and appeal.
What the player does and why; the player, not the game, drives it forward.
Appeal: the pull to keep playing. It is the hardest to guarantee, and the most important.

slides.title: Communication and guiding the focus
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Random walk with step 14 px and a fixed seed against a straight walk to the door.
slides.picture: A room with a hidden door. Without a clue the player wanders. With a lit door they walk straight to it.

new_texts: Showing the player the goal and how to reach it, with clues in the environment.
tell them where to look now
Nothing says where the goal is. The player wanders: this run takes 2476 steps. (A seeded random walk.)
all_texts: Showing the player the goal and how to reach it, with clues in the environment.
tell them where to look now
Nothing says where the goal is. The player wanders: this run takes 2476 steps. (A seeded random walk.)

new_texts: Making clear what the player should concentrate on.
WITH A CLUE: THE DOOR IS LIT
A lit door and a ring of light draw the eye. The same player now needs 43 steps. Guiding the focus means making the next thing to look at obvious.

slides.title: Linear, nonlinear and side quest
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Routes: 1 for linear; 2 x 2 = 4 with two forks.
slides.picture: A straight chain of rooms, then a chain with two forks, then a side quest loop leaving and rejoining the main line.

new_texts: Straight from start to end, or with alternate choices along the way.
one route from start to end
Linear: each room leads to the next. Easy to guide, and the designer controls the pace.
all_texts: Straight from start to end, or with alternate choices along the way.
one route from start to end
Linear: each room leads to the next. Easy to guide, and the designer controls the pace.

new_texts: Nonlinear: two forks give 2 × 2 = 4 routes. The player must be given alternatives, not one corridor.
all_texts: Straight from start to end, or with alternate choices along the way.
one route from start to end
Nonlinear: two forks give 2 × 2 = 4 routes. The player must be given alternatives, not one corridor.

new_texts: A detour from the main storyline.
Main line plus an optional detour: 2 ways to finish (with or without it).
A side quest is a detour off the main story. It returns to the same line, so the main story still holds.

new_texts: Planning and building the spaces the player moves through.
The first level lets the player try each skill, with no text.
the space shows what to do

new_texts: Build the engaging middle levels, then the opening levels that lead there.
ORDER OF DESIGN AGAINST ORDER OF PLAY
The middle is built first, then the start that leads into it.
Designing the middle first shows what players can do. Then the opening levels are built to lead them there.

slides.title: Anticipation and build-up
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Reaction time 0.25 s is an assumption. Curves are illustrative powers of time.
slides.picture: A timeline of an enemy attack with and without a 0.5 second wind-up, then three curves for sound, sparks and camera shake rising to an explosion.

new_texts: Prepare the player for what comes next, such as a wind-up before an attack.
a short warning before the hit
a long rise toward the event
TIME FROM FIRST SIGN TO DAMAGE
Reaction time of 0.25 s is an assumption.
no time to react: it feels cheap
time to spare after reacting: 0.25 s
A 0.5 s wind-up leaves 0.25 s to react after a 0.25 s reaction. No wind-up leaves none, and the player feels cheated.
all_texts: Prepare the player for what comes next, such as a wind-up before an attack.
a short warning before the hit
a long rise toward the event

time to spare after reacting: 0.25 s

new_texts: A sequence that raises tension toward an event: sound, sparks, camera shake.
At 90% of the way: sound 0.85, sparks 0.81, shake 0.73.
Illustrative curves; the shake arrives last.
Before the explosion: sound builds, sparks fly, the camera starts to shake. The whole scene is one long build-up.

slides.title: Logical events and consistent rules
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Bounce heights: 100 x 0.8^n against seeded random values.
slides.picture: A table of player actions and the expected responses, then two rows of bounce heights: one consistent, one random.

new_texts: Events behave sensibly and meet the player's unspoken expectations.
Shoot a wall and a bullet hole should appear. Walk on gravel and it should crunch. If not, the player's expectation is broken.
all_texts: Events behave sensibly and meet the player's unspoken expectations.
Shoot a wall and a bullet hole should appear. Walk on gravel and it should crunch. If not, the player's expectation is broken.

new_texts: Even where physics is bent, it is bent the same way every time.
PEAK HEIGHT OF EACH BOUNCE (PERCENT OF THE DROP)
A game may change physics, but the same way every time. The first row can be learned. The second cannot.
all_texts: Events behave sensibly and meet the player's unspoken expectations.

slides.title: Games can cheat
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Distances in pixels; the 120 px turn trigger is illustrative.
slides.picture: A top-down view. A guard faces away and the player sneaks up from behind. An honest guard turns and catches the player. A guard told not to turn lets the player ambush.

new_texts: Hidden help the player does not notice, such as enemies told not to turn around.
reacts to everything it could sense
the guard turned and saw you
An honest guard hears and sees all around it. At 120 px it turns, and the sneak fails.
all_texts: Hidden help the player does not notice, such as enemies told not to turn around.
reacts to everything it could sense
the guard turned and saw you
An honest guard hears and sees all around it. At 120 px it turns, and the sneak fails.

new_texts: THE GUARD IS TOLD NOT TO TURN
The designers told this guard not to turn around. The player can ambush from behind, and the game rewards that play. As long as the player does not notice, it works.

slides.title: Dynamic play
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Durations 3, 5, 3 and 7 s with start times 0, 1, 2 and 0.
slides.picture: A timeline of four team actions in a bomb round, overlapping in the first step and placed one after another in the second.

new_texts: Many things happening at once, so play stays fresh.
Total time 8 s, up to 4 things happening at once.
A smoke, a flank, a charge and an angle check all overlap. The round is full, and the defenders must watch everything.
all_texts: Many things happening at once, so play stays fresh.
Total time 8 s, up to 4 things happening at once.
A smoke, a flank, a charge and an angle check all overlap. The round is full, and the defenders must watch everything.

new_texts: Total time 18 s, never more than 1 thing happening.
Do the same four things one after another: 18 s and one thing at a time. Easy to predict, and dull.

slides.title: Progression, pacing and waves
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm); Crash Course Games, “Game Design”.
slides.notes: Intensity curves are illustrative; time in band is computed from them.
slides.picture: A line chart of intensity over four minutes with a comfortable band. A steady climb leaves the band. Alternating calm and intense stays inside it. Then two ways to build one wave of strength ten.

new_texts: A natural rise in challenge; do not over-stimulate or under-stimulate.
Time inside the band: 56% of the four minutes
Progression should climb, but a straight climb over-stimulates the player near the end.
all_texts: A natural rise in challenge; do not over-stimulate or under-stimulate.
Time inside the band: 56% of the four minutes
Progression should climb, but a straight climb over-stimulates the player near the end.

new_texts: WAVES OF HIGH AND LOW INTENSITY
Time inside the band: 88% of the four minutes
Peaks then rests keep the player in the band while still rising.
Pacing alternates. The tower defence game alternates waves of enemies with time to build, so the player never saturates.

slides.title: Spacing
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Three characters drifting in two rooms with a fixed seed; contact when closer than 40 px.
slides.picture: Two rooms of the same length, one three times as tall. Three characters drift around. In the tight room they bump into each other far more often.

new_texts: Open areas to admire, or tight ones that feel claustrophobic; leave room for AI.
Open: 7.0 square metres each. The characters rarely touch, and the player has room to look around.
all_texts: Open areas to admire, or tight ones that feel claustrophobic; leave room for AI.
Open: 7.0 square metres each. The characters rarely touch, and the player has room to look around.

new_texts: Tight: 2.3 square metres each. They touch in 72 of 300 frames, against 17 in the open room. Narrow space changes the pace, and AI needs room to move.

slides.title: Before you call the pacing done
slides.source: Source: a game design tips video (title to confirm); Crash Course Games, “Game Design”.
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Does the player know their role, the goal and how to reach it?
Can they tell where to look, and do they have alternatives?
Is every danger telegraphed, and do events behave as expected?
Are the rules consistent, and is any cheating hidden and helpful?
Does the pace alternate and still rise, inside a comfortable band?
Is there room to move, or tightness on purpose?
Then say it exactly: not “the level feels flat”, but “60 s of enemies, 30 s of calm”.
